newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kohl, others call for Romania in NATO first wave. [CORRECTED 21:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kohl, others call for Romania in NATO first wave. [CORRECTED 21:45 GMT]

text.p: European centrist leaders including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl called on Tuesday for Romania to be included in the first wave of new NATO members.

Wilfried Martens, former Belgian prime minister and head of the European Peoples' Party (EPP), said after a summit of the mainly Christian Democrat group that Romania should begin negotiations this year for membership in 1999.
"Everybody, above all the heads of government, supported Romania's candidacy in the first wave," Martens told reporters.

He said the group, which includes the heads of government of NATO members Germany, Spain, Italy, Luxembourg and Belgium. had pledged to try to overcome U.S. reluctance to Romania as one of the first new NATO members from the former Communist east.
The U.S. Senate, fearful of the costs, is particularly reluctant to see a large group of new members joining the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in the near future.
But Martens said the Christian Democrats, Europe's second largest political movement, wanted Bucharest in NATO soon.
"If that is not possible we will demand that a date must be fixed for the second wave which will include Romania," Martens said.
Kohl, Italy's Romano Prodi, Belgium's Jean-Luc Dehaene and Luxembourg's Jean-Claude Juncker all attended the meeting, along with Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes.
Earlier the group held brief talks with Romanian Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea.

NATO is due to announce at a summit in Madrid on July 8 and 9 (Corrects from July 7 and 8) the names of the first countries from eastern Europe that will be invited to begin negotiations for membership in 1999.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are widely tipped to be the front runners, with Slovenia and Romania often mentioned as outside chances.
Martens said Slovenia had not been mentioned at the meeting.
France, which has lonstanding cultural ties with Romania, has been pushing hard for its inclusion in the first wave.
